description: RFC 8785 JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS) cases for the FPP plugin coordinator contract, docs/build/FPP-PLUGIN-COORDINATOR-CONTRACTS.md section 1.3. Each case's expectedCanonical and expectedSha256 are frozen contract expectations, generated once from pkg/fppidentity.Canonicalize and HashCanonical and re-checked against the plugin repository's native/src/json.cpp. A consumer runs its own canonicalizer over input and compares byte for byte against expectedCanonical, then hashes those bytes and compares against expectedSha256.

cases.name: duplicate-sequence-name-playlist
cases.description: A realistic FPP playlist definition with a name, desc, repeat, and a mainPlaylist array where two entries (chorus.fseq) share an identical sequenceName at different positions with different mediaName and duration. This is the duplicate-filename case the entry-key design exists for: sequenceName alone cannot identify an entry.

cases.name: duplicate-sequence-name-playlist-reordered
cases.description: The same playlist definition as duplicate-sequence-name-playlist, with the mainPlaylist entries reordered and every object's own members shuffled and re-spaced. The canonical form and hash differ from duplicate-sequence-name-playlist because array element order is significant even though object member order is not.

cases.name: duplicate-sequence-name-playlist-edited
cases.description: The same playlist definition as duplicate-sequence-name-playlist with one field edited: the second chorus.fseq entry's duration changes from 28 to 29. The hash differs from both duplicate-sequence-name-playlist and duplicate-sequence-name-playlist-reordered.

cases.name: member-name-utf16-vs-utf8-sort
cases.description: Two single-character member names, U+E000 (a 3-byte UTF-8 sequence) and U+10000 (a supplementary character encoded as a 4-byte UTF-8 sequence, a UTF-16 surrogate pair). RFC 8785 requires sorting by UTF-16 code unit, under which U+10000's surrogate pair (starting at 0xD800) sorts before U+E000. Raw UTF-8 byte order disagrees and would sort them the other way, so this case fails under a byte-order sort.

cases.name: nested-objects-and-arrays
cases.description: An object containing an array that itself contains a nested object, exercising recursive canonicalization: the outer object's members sort, the array's element order is preserved, and the nested object's members sort independently.

cases.name: string-escapes-and-control-character
cases.description: A string containing every named JSON escape (quote, backslash, backspace, form feed, newline, carriage return, tab), a solidus (which JCS does not escape on output), and a control character below 0x20 with no named escape (vertical tab, 0x0b), which must render as \u000b.

cases.name: number-formatting
cases.description: ECMAScript Number::toString formatting boundary cases in one array: 0 and -0 both render as 0, an ordinary integer, 1e21 (the boundary where JCS switches to exponential notation), 1e-7 (exponential) and 1e-6 (the boundary where it switches back to plain decimal), and the largest finite float64 (1.7976931348623157e+308), which needs all 17 significant digits to round-trip.

cases.name: duplicate-member-names
cases.description: An object with the member name "a" repeated. JCS gives no canonical answer for which duplicate should survive, so this must be rejected rather than silently resolved by keeping the first or last occurrence.

cases.name: malformed-json
cases.description: Structurally invalid JSON (an unterminated object with no member name). Must be rejected, not repaired.

cases.name: depth-200-nested-arrays-empty-innermost
cases.description: Exactly 200 nested arrays (the accepted boundary, pkg/fppidentity maxDepth=200), innermost array empty. Only container entry counts toward depth, so this must be accepted; the plugin's C++ parser (which checks the bound at the top of parseValue) never evaluates the check for an empty innermost container either, so this pins the half of the depth contract both implementations already agree on.

cases.name: depth-200-nested-arrays-scalar-innermost
cases.description: Exactly 200 nested arrays (the accepted boundary), with a scalar 0 in the innermost array so it is non-empty. Pins the same accepted boundary as depth-200-nested-arrays-empty-innermost under the variant where the innermost container's own parseValue call (as the plugin's C++ parser performs it) actually runs.

cases.name: depth-201-nested-arrays-empty-innermost
cases.description: 201 nested arrays, one past the accepted boundary, with the innermost array empty. The coordinator's Go parser checks the depth bound immediately on entering parseArray, so this must be refused even with an empty innermost container. This is the shape the recorded off-by-one divergence turns on: the plugin's C++ parser checks depth_ > kMaxDepth at the top of parseValue, so a container with no elements never has parseValue called for a first element, and the plugin accepts this shape. See docs/build/FPP-PLUGIN-COORDINATOR-CONTRACTS.md section 1.3.

cases.name: depth-201-nested-arrays-scalar-innermost
cases.description: 201 nested arrays, one past the accepted boundary, with a scalar 0 in the innermost array so it is non-empty. Both the coordinator and the plugin refuse this shape: the non-empty innermost container triggers the plugin's parseValue depth check on its first element. Pins the half of the depth contract that already agrees, which a future refactor could break silently if only the empty-innermost pair were pinned.

cases.name: invalid-utf8-string-value
cases.description: A string value containing a single lone 0x80 continuation byte with no preceding lead byte, an invalid UTF-8 sequence. Carried as inputHex, not input: a JSON string cannot hold a byte that is not valid UTF-8 without an RFC 8259-compliant decoder silently replacing it with U+FFFD before this coordinator's canonicalizer ever sees it (see README.md). The coordinator refuses (contract section 1.3); the plugin's C++ parser accepts this and passes the raw bytes through, so the two sides diverge here until the plugin's own fix, which also needs inputHex support, lands.

cases.name: invalid-utf8-member-name
cases.description: An object member name containing a single lone 0x80 continuation byte, an invalid UTF-8 sequence. Carried as inputHex for the same reason as invalid-utf8-string-value. The coordinator refuses (contract section 1.3); the plugin's C++ parser accepts this and passes the raw bytes through, so the two sides diverge here until the plugin's own fix, which also needs inputHex support, lands.

cases.name: inputhex-valid-utf8-positive-control
cases.description: A positive control for the inputHex field itself: perfectly valid UTF-8 bytes (an ASCII member alongside a member whose string value is café, e with an acute accent, a 2-byte UTF-8 sequence) carried as inputHex and expected to succeed exactly like an equivalent input case would. Exists so a consumer that ignores inputHex entirely (and would therefore also silently pass invalid-utf8-string-value and invalid-utf8-member-name by treating them as empty input) is caught here first: an all-refusal inputHex suite proves nothing about whether inputHex is actually read.
